title: Dependency-Aware Discrete Diffusion for Scene Graph Generation

paper.title: Dependency-Aware Discrete Diffusion for Scene Graph Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Scene graphs (SGs) represent objects and their relationships as structured graphs, enabling applications in image generation, robotics, and 3D understanding.
Recent work suggests that conditioning image generation on scene graphs improves compositional fidelity compared to text-only prompting.
However, since users typically provide text rather than structured graphs, a key challenge is to generate scene graphs from natural language.
Prior work on discrete diffusion has demonstrated success in generating generic graphs such as molecules and circuits, but fails to account for the hierarchical structure and strong dependencies between objects, edges, and relations in scene graphs.
We address this limitation by introducing a dependency-aware, hierarchically constrained discrete diffusion model for scene graph generation.
Our approach decouples structure and semantics across the forward and reverse processes, enabling the model to capture conditional dependencies.
At inference time, we perform training-free conditioning to sample text-aligned scene graphs.
We evaluate our method on standard SG benchmarks and demonstrate improvements over both continuous and discrete graph generation baselines across graph and layout metrics.
When fed to downstream image generation, our approach yields improved compositional alignment compared to text-to-image models, particularly in multi-object scenarios.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Text-to-image (T2I) models have made remarkable progress in generating images from user-specified prompts, but user expectations are rising just as quickly. As prompts become longer and more complex, multiple lines of attack are being explored to improve compositional fidelity and alignment. Figure 1: Image I I and its scene graph G G . Objects are pink nodes and relations are labels on edges. One promising direction is to generate images from scene graphs (SGs)—see Fig. 1 —where visual objects are represented as nodes and their relationships as edges. Recent papers Xu et al. (2024) ; Farshad et al. (2023) ; Thanh-Nhan et al. (2025) ; Shen and Lin (2025) suggest that SG-conditioned image generation p ⁡ ( I | G ) p(I|G) can be more effective, particularly in compositional settings. While these gains are largely empirical, they are intuitively justified: text-based conditioning lacks explicit relational constraints, often leading to compositional inconsistencies. In contrast, scene graphs provide an explicit factorization over objects and relations, offering a structured prior that is difficult to encode in text embeddings. Given this momentum, a natural question arises: how can scene graphs (SG) be generated from text prompts? While text-to-SG mapping may appear deterministic, it is inherently multi-modal due to the ambiguity and under-specification of natural language. For example, a prompt such as “a person and a surfboard” does not specify their relationship; the person could be on, beside, or holding the surfboard. Multiple valid SGs may correspond to the same prompt, necessitating modeling a conditional distribution p ⁡ ( G | T ) p(G|T) rather than predicting a single deterministic output. Motivated by this, we propose to learn the manifold of scene graphs using discrete diffusion models, and then perform conditional generation of SGs from text prompts. However, this presents a fundamental challenge: scene graphs are significantly more complex than generic graphs. They exhibit long-tailed vocabularies, strong conditional dependencies between objects and relations, and global structural constraints. Injecting these properties into discrete diffusion remains underexplored. A key limitation of existing discrete diffusion approaches Vignac et al. (2023) —designed for generic graphs like molecules or traffic networks—is that they rely on parameterizations that treat nodes and edges as independent categorical variables in both the forward and reverse processes. With scene graphs, such independence assumptions break due to the inherent conditional dependencies, such as the hierarchical structure where objects determine edges and edges determine relations. Our key insight is that scene graphs require a hierarchically constrained discrete diffusion process , where structure and semantics are modeled with explicit conditional dependencies rather than independent categorical transitions. Across these benchmarks, our method outperforms both continuous SG generation models and prior discrete graph baselines while achieving competitive performance on layout prediction. sections.text: Discrete Diffusion. Continuous diffusion Song et al. (2021) ; Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015) , typically using a Gaussian noising process, is not well-suited for categorical or structured data such as graphs. This motivates diffusion directly in discrete state spaces. In discrete diffusion Austin et al. (2023) , each entity takes values in a finite set of K K categories. The forward process is defined via transition matrices { Q t } t = 1 T \{Q_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} , where, q ⁡ ( x t ∣ x t − 1 ) = x t − 1 ​ Q t , q(x_{t}\mid x_{t-1})=x_{t-1}Q_{t}, and the marginal at time t t is given by, q ⁡ ( x t ∣ x 0 ) = x 0 ​ Q ¯ t , Q ¯ t = ∏ s = 1 t Q s . q(x_{t}\mid x_{0})=x_{0}\bar{Q}_{t},\hskip 10.00002pt\bar{Q}_{t}=\prod_{s=1}^{t}Q_{s}. Discrete Diffusion on Graphs. DiGress Vignac et al. (2023) extends discrete diffusion to graphs by modeling node and edge attributes as independent categorical variables. A graph is represented as G = ( V , E ) G=(V,E) , and the forward process is defined by, q ⁡ ( G t ∣ G t − 1 ) = ( V t − 1 ​ Q t V , E t − 1 ​ Q t E ) , q(G_{t}\mid G_{t-1})=\big(V_{t-1}Q^{V}_{t},\;E_{t-1}Q^{E}_{t}\big), with closed-form marginals, q ⁡ ( G t ∣ G 0 ) = ( V 0 ​ Q ¯ t V , E 0 ​ Q ¯ t E ) . q(G_{t}\mid G_{0})=\big(V_{0}\bar{Q}^{V}_{t},\;E_{0}\bar{Q}^{E}_{t}\big). The reverse model predicts clean node and edge distributions, and sampling proceeds independently across nodes and edges, p θ ​ ( G t − 1 ∣ G t ) = ∏ i p θ ​ ( v t − 1 i ∣ G t ) ​ ∏ i , j p θ ​ ( e t − 1 i ​ j ∣ G t ) . p_{\theta}(G_{t-1}\mid G_{t})=\prod_{i}p_{\theta}(v^{i}_{t-1}\mid G_{t})\prod_{i,j}p_{\theta}(e^{ij}_{t-1}\mid G_{t}). (1) Each term is computed by marginalizing over predicted clean states (nodes & edges), p θ ​ ( v t − 1 i ∣ G t ) = ∑ v 0 q ⁡ ( v t − 1 i ∣ v 0 , x t i ) ​ p ^ V i ​ ( v 0 ) , p θ ​ ( v t − 1 i ∣ v 0 , G t ) = { q ⁡ ( v t − 1 i ∣ v 0 , x t i ) , if ​ q ​ ( x t i ∣ v 0 ) > 0 , 0 , otherwise . p_{\theta}(v^{i}_{t-1}\mid G_{t})=\sum_{v_{0}}q(v^{i}_{t-1}\mid v_{0},x^{i}_{t})\,\hat{p}^{i}_{V}(v_{0}),\hskip 20.00003ptp_{\theta}(v^{i}_{t-1}\mid v_{0},G_{t})=\begin{cases}q(v^{i}_{t-1}\mid v_{0},x^{i}_{t}),&\text{if }q(x^{i}_{t}\mid v_{0})>0,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (2) This formulation enforces permutation invariance, and treats nodes and edges as independent categorical variables. However, it assumes a categorical space where edge existence and semantics, edge identity are coupled, which is unsuitable for scene graphs’ strong inter-entity dependence, large relation vocabularies, and long-tailed relation distribution.

sections.text: DiScGraph ’s redesign of discrete diffusion entails 4 4 parts, starting with a (1) hierarchical representation of SGs, (2) an edge-gated forward noising process (3) a factorized reverse sampler for unconditional generation, and (4) a text-conditioned SG generation at inference time (see Fig. 2 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 Hierarchical Scene Graph Representation
sections.text: In discrete diffusion, a graph is represented as a flat categorical state G = ( V , E ) G=(V,E) , where node labels V V and edge labels E E are independently modeled Vignac et al. (2023) . While this representation is effective for, say, molecules or transportation graphs (where edge relations are defined over a small, well-defined vocabulary with strict constraints), SGs involve large, long-tailed relational vocabularies and strong object–relation dependencies. Modeling the edges with a single categorical variable, say e i ​ j ∈ { n ​ o ​ E ​ d ​ g ​ e , r 1 , r 2 , … , r K } e_{ij}\in\{noEdge,r_{1},r_{2},\dots,r_{K}\} , biases the learning towards edges rather than relations, especially for sparse scene graphs, large K K , and the long-tailed distribution over relation classes r k r_{k} . Scene graphs are better modeled by separating edges (structure) from the relations (semantics), so that relations can be conditioned only on active edges , i.e., e i ​ j = 0 ⇒ r i ​ j = 0 e_{ij}=0\Rightarrow r_{ij}=0 . This motivates our decoupled representation in which each edge is factorized into two: (i) edge existence, e i ​ j ∈ { 0 , 1 } e_{ij}\in\{0,1\} , and (ii) relation identity, r i ​ j + ∈ { 1 , … , K r ​ e ​ l } r^{+}_{ij}\in\{1,\dots,K_{rel}\} . (4) Thus the abstract graph state space 𝒢 := 𝒱 N × { 0 , … , K r ​ e ​ l } N × N \mathcal{G}:=\mathcal{V}^{N}\times\{0,\dots,K_{rel}\}^{N\times N} is modified to the constrained scene graph space, 𝒮 ​ 𝒢 := 𝒱 N × { 0 , 1 } N × N × { 1 , … , K r ​ e ​ l } N × N \mathcal{SG}:=\mathcal{V}^{N}\times\{0,1\}^{N\times N}\times\{1,\dots,K_{rel}\}^{N\times N} . sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: ■ \blacksquare Datasets : We train the scene graph generator on popular scene graph datasets: Visual Genome (VG) Krishna et al. (2016) , COCO-Stuff Lin et al. (2015) , and a large-scale dataset LAION-SG Li et al. (2024) . Both quantitative and qualitative results reported are from evaluations on VG/COCO-validation and CompSGBench Li et al. (2024) benchmark, consisting of SGs describing complex multi-object-relation visual scenes. ■ \blacksquare Image Generators : For T2I generation task, we use SG-to-image generator SDXL-SG Li et al. (2024) , and Layout-to-image generator, GLIGEN Li et al. (2023) . ■ \blacksquare Baselines : (1) Graph Generators : We compare generated unconditional SGs against generic diffusion graph generators trained on SG datasets: DiGress Vignac et al. (2023) , GraphGDP Huang et al. (2022) , D3PM Austin et al. (2023) , autoregressive SG generators: SceneGraphGen Garg et al. (2021) and VarScene Verma et al. (2022) , and diffusion SG work: DiffuseSG Xu et al. (2024) . (2) Layout Generators : We compare layouts extracted from DiScGraph ’s layout head against Transformer model: BLT Kong et al. (2022) , discrete diffusion works: LayoutDiffusion Zhou et al. (2023) , LayoutDM Inoue et al. (2023) that generate discretized layouts trained on layouts from SG datasets, and DiffuseSG Xu et al. (2024) that generates layouts along with scene graphs. (3) T2I Image Generation : We compare text-conditioned SG to image generation performance against text-only compositional works: ComposedDiff Liu et al. (2023) , CO3 Dutta et al. (2026) on SDXL, and base SDXL Podell et al. (2023) . We also compare layout-to-image generation with LLM augmented works: LayoutLLM-T2I Qu et al. (2023) , and LDM Lian et al. (2024) . ■ \blacksquare Metrics : We use (1) Unconditional Graph Metrics : N-MMD , R-MMD , ID-MMD , OD-MMD Xu et al. (2024) (for baselines, relations and edges are synonymous). A triplet is defined as < object,relation,subject >, and Triplet-TV measures if semantic consistency is preserved. Attach-TV (AT-TV) measures how accurately the model generates relations that "attach" to given objects. RARE-K-TV (R-K-TV) measures the model’s capability to generate long-tailed relations. (2) Layout Metrics : F1 scores between generated and ground truth layouts. (3) Image Quality Metrics : FID , CLIP-I2I , CLIP-I2T Radford et al. (2021) , BLIP-VQA Huang et al. (2023) , and ImageReward (IR) Xu et al. (2023) . (4) Scene-graph-to-image metrics: SG-IoU , Entity-IoU , Relation-IoU Shen et al. (2024) , that measure structural overlap between generated and real images; quantified via IoU of SGs, objects, and relations extracted by an LLM from the image pairs. ■ \blacksquare Training Details : We use the graph transformer Yun et al. (2020) backbone for the denoiser ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} , following DiGress Vignac et al. (2023) . However, the embeddings and denoiser prediction heads are modified for the SG factorized formulation. Additionally, we also use a layout head that extracts layouts from sampled scene graphs. GIoU layout loss ensures a geometrically consistent scene graph generator. Please refer to Appendix Sec. A.4 for more details on metrics and implementation details.

sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: ■ \blacksquare Deep Graph Generative Models: Pre-diffusion autoregressive, VAE, and GAN graph generators You et al. (2018) ; Liao et al. (2019) ; Samanta et al. (2019) ; Li et al. (2018b) ; Ingraham et al. (2019) ; Simonovsky and Komodakis (2018) ; De Cao and Kipf (2018) impose special constraints like node ordering, unlabelled, fixed-size graphs, poor scaling, and training instabilities. Concurrently, many works explored scene graph generation (VarScene, SceneGraphGen) Verma et al. (2022) ; Garg et al. (2021) and prediction Newell and Deng (2017) ; Li et al. (2018a) ; Xu et al. (2017) ; Yang et al. (2018) ; Zellers et al. (2018) tasks. ■ \blacksquare Diffusion Graph Generation. (1) Continuous: Diffusion models have replaced autoregressive approaches as the SOTA graph modeling paradigm. Early graph diffusion models Niu et al. (2020) , Jo et al. (2022) , Huang et al. (2022) applied thresholding to snap continuous generations to categorical. DiffuseSG Xu et al. (2024) adapts this idea for grounded scene graphs. Grounding augments standard scene graphs’ node-object representation to include layouts. The rationale is layout is continuous while graph components are discrete, so grounded SGs are treated as continuous. (2) Discrete diffusion models: Following the success of discrete diffusion for text, audio, point clouds etc. Trippe et al. (2023) ; Hoogeboom et al. (2022) ; Wu and Li (2023) , DiGress Vignac et al. (2023) designs a discrete diffusion model for abstract graphs (molecules, traffic, etc.). The forward process corrupts nodes and edges independently. The training enforces permutation invariance, and DiGress produces exchangeable graph distributions. While this works well for abstract graphs, scene graphs are inherently directed, have large vocabularies, long-tailed relation distributions, and expect semantic consistency between objects and relations. Our work DiScGraph addresses these scene graph-specific requirements with a hierarchical constrained factorized state space and corresponding factorized reverse sampler. ■ \blacksquare Controllable Image Generation: (1) Layout & LLM-augmented methods: Layout generation works ( Xie et al., 2023 ; Kong et al., 2022 ; Inoue et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ) use autoregressive and discrete diffusion paradigms to generate layouts or leverage LLM reasoning to infer layouts from text ( Qu et al., 2023 ; Lian et al., 2024 ) , With backbones like GLIGEN Li et al. (2023) , ControlNet Zhang et al. (2023) , they can generate layout-to-image. (2) T2I Composition works: such as Composed-Diffusion ( Liu et al., 2023 ) and CO3 Dutta et al. (2026) enable algebraic composition of text concepts to rectify misaligned attributes. (3) SG-to-Image: Several works Johnson et al. (2018) ; Yang et al. (2022) ; Farshad et al. (2023) train specific SG-to-image generators. SG-Adapter Shen et al. (2024) introduces SG IP-adapter that activates SG conditioning in existing image models. SDXL-SG Li et al. (2024) trains a large-scale SOTA image generator SDXL conditioned on scene graphs. SGEdit Zhang et al. (2024) performs SG-to-image editing, and SGDiff Zhang et al. (2025) generates SG to image captions.

sections.heading: 6 Limitations & Future Scope
sections.text: We designed a scene graph generator as a factorized discrete diffusion model, DiScGraph , that has a factorized state space decoupling structure from semantics for better relation learning and a dependency-aware reverse sampler to sample SGs with strong entity dependence. Furthermore, we facilitated text-conditioned scene graph generation by sampling from a text-reward tilted distribution. The text-conditioned model was then used downstream in image generation. We provided empirical evidence on T2I generation improvements, unconditional scene graph generation metrics, and layout metrics. While DiScGraph achieves good scene graph generation and T2I generation performance, there is room for improvement, (1) Our text conditioning framework operates at inference time through reward-tilted sampling, avoiding conditional model retraining. While this works well for textual abstractions – SGs, the quality of conditioning depends heavily on the reward function (CLIP). Future work could explore stronger learned reward models. (2) Graph transformers scale quadratically with the number of scene entities and relations. While practical for current scene graph datasets, scaling to very large structured scenes may require techniques like sparse attention. (3) Discrete frameworks are restricted by sampler quality, requiring sampling refinements (Sec. A.2.2 , A.4.2 ). For future work, we plan to address it in a more principled way by designing a robust sampling algorithm. (4) Layout prediction can become ambiguous for scene graphs with many disconnected sub-graphs. Future work could explore a latent layout generation that models multiple plausible global layouts conditioned on the same SG. (5) Scene graph quality is dependent on the text input and is encumbered by unexpressive text prompts, limiting improvements to image generation. Limited availability of large-scale scene graph data and scene graph conditioned image generators also limits development; however, recent efforts like LAION-SG Li et al. (2024) are a step in the right direction.

(56) For binary edges, p ⁡ ( e i ​ j , t = b ∣ e i ​ j , 0 ) = [ e i ​ j , 0 ​ Q ¯ t E ] b . p(e_{ij,t}=b\mid e_{ij,0})=\left[e_{ij,0}\,\bar{Q}_{t}^{E}\right]_{b}. (57)

sections.heading: Closed-form marginal for relations.
sections.text: The relation marginals need to be reworked for the factorized scene graph space 𝒮 ​ 𝒢 \mathcal{SG} . Relation marginals depend on the edge state at time t t . Conditioned on an active edge, q ⁡ ( r i ​ j , t ∣ r i ​ j , 0 , e i ​ j , t = 1 ) = Cat ⁡ ( r i ​ j , 0 ​ Q ¯ t R ) , q(r_{ij,t}\mid r_{ij,0},e_{ij,t}=1)=\mathrm{Cat}\!\left(r_{ij,0}\,\bar{Q}_{t}^{R}\right), (58) where Q ¯ t R = Q 1 R Q 2 R ⋯ Q t R \bar{Q}_{t}^{R}=Q_{1}^{R}Q_{2}^{R}\cdots Q_{t}^{R} . If the edge is inactive, q ⁡ ( r i ​ j , t = 0 ∣ r i ​ j , 0 , e i ​ j , t = 0 ) = 1 . q(r_{ij,t}=0\mid r_{ij,0},e_{ij,t}=0)=1. (59) Thus, the structural components, edges, are decoupled from the semantics, relations, but the dependency structure ensures we are operating in valid scene graph space. q ⁡ ( r i ​ j , t ∣ r i ​ j , 0 , e i ​ j , t ) = { Cat ⁡ ( r i ​ j , 0 ​ Q ¯ t R ) , e i ​ j , t = 1 , δ 0 ​ ( r i ​ j , t ) , e i ​ j , t = 0 . q(r_{ij,t}\mid r_{ij,0},e_{ij,t})=\begin{cases}\mathrm{Cat}\!\left(r_{ij,0}\,\bar{Q}_{t}^{R}\right),&e_{ij,t}=1,\\ \delta_{0}(r_{ij,t}),&e_{ij,t}=0.\end{cases} (60)

sections.heading: Full closed-form marginal.
sections.text: Combining all components, q ⁡ ( x t ∣ x 0 ) = q V ​ ( V t ∣ V 0 ) ​ q E ​ ( E t ∣ E 0 ) ​ q R ​ ( R t ∣ R 0 , E t ) . q(x_{t}\mid x_{0})=q_{V}(V_{t}\mid V_{0})\,q_{E}(E_{t}\mid E_{0})\,q_{R}(R_{t}\mid R_{0},E_{t}). (61) q ⁡ ( x t ∣ x 0 ) \displaystyle q(x_{t}\mid x_{0}) = ∏ i q V ​ ( v i , t ∣ v i , 0 ) ​ ∏ i ≠ j q E ​ ( e i ​ j , t ∣ e i ​ j , 0 ) \displaystyle=\prod_{i}q_{V}(v_{i,t}\mid v_{i,0})\prod_{i\neq j}q_{E}(e_{ij,t}\mid e_{ij,0}) (62) ⋅ ∏ i ​ j : e i ​ j , t = 1 q R ( r i ​ j , t ∣ r i ​ j , 0 , e i ​ j , t = 1 ) ∏ i ​ j : e i ​ j , t = 0 δ 0 ( r i ​ j , t ) . \displaystyle\cdot\prod_{ij:e_{ij,t}=1}q_{R}(r_{ij,t}\mid r_{ij,0},e_{ij,t}=1)\prod_{ij:e_{ij,t}=0}\delta_{0}(r_{ij,t}). This enables direct sampling of noisy states of the factorized space during training.

sections.heading: Absorbing-mask corruption.
sections.text: Given the success of absorbing masks for diffusion language tasks, apart from random corruption, we apply absorbing mask corruption, which preserves the structure and only deletes information (object and relation), allowing the model to specifically learn semantics, which is beneficial for scene graphs. We define mask tokens [ MASK ] V [\mathrm{MASK}]_{V} and [ MASK ] R [\mathrm{MASK}]_{R} . For objects: q V ​ ( v i , t ∣ v i , t − 1 ) = ( 1 − β t V ) ​ δ v i , t − 1 + β t V ​ δ [ MASK ] V . q_{V}(v_{i,t}\mid v_{i,t-1})=(1-\beta_{t}^{V})\delta_{v_{i,t-1}}+\beta_{t}^{V}\delta_{[\mathrm{MASK}]_{V}}. (63) For relations on active edges: q ~ R ​ ( r i ​ j , t ∣ r i ​ j , t − 1 ) = ( 1 − β t R ) ​ δ r i ​ j , t − 1 + β t R ​ δ [ MASK ] R . \tilde{q}_{R}(r_{ij,t}\mid r_{ij,t-1})=(1-\beta_{t}^{R})\delta_{r_{ij,t-1}}+\beta_{t}^{R}\delta_{[\mathrm{MASK}]_{R}}. (64) The edge-aware kernel becomes q R ​ ( r i ​ j , t ∣ r i ​ j , t − 1 , e i ​ j , t ) = { ( 1 − β t R ) ​ δ r i ​ j , t − 1 + β t R ​ δ [ MASK ] R , e i ​ j , t = 1 , δ 0 ​ ( r i ​ j , t ) , e i ​ j , t = 0 . q_{R}(r_{ij,t}\mid r_{ij,t-1},e_{ij,t})=\begin{cases}(1-\beta_{t}^{R})\delta_{r_{ij,t-1}}+\beta_{t}^{R}\delta_{[\mathrm{MASK}]_{R}},&e_{ij,t}=1,\\ \delta_{0}(r_{ij,t}),&e_{ij,t}=0.\end{cases} (65) This restricts masking to valid relations.

sections.heading: Hybrid random + mask corruption.
sections.text: Performing masking in isolation would not allow the model to learn structure; we need a hybrid kernel combining random replacement and mask absorption, thereby learning both structure and semantics. For objects: q V ​ ( v i , t ∣ v i , t − 1 ) = ( 1 − β t V ) ​ δ v i , t − 1 + β t V ​ [ ρ V ​ δ [ MASK ] V + ( 1 − ρ V ) ​ π V ] . q_{V}(v_{i,t}\mid v_{i,t-1})=(1-\beta_{t}^{V})\delta_{v_{i,t-1}}+\beta_{t}^{V}\big[\rho_{V}\delta_{[\mathrm{MASK}]_{V}}+(1-\rho_{V})\pi_{V}\big]. (66) For active relations: q ~ R ​ ( r i ​ j , t ∣ r i ​ j , t − 1 ) = ( 1 − β t R ) ​ δ r i ​ j , t − 1 + β t R ​ [ ρ R ​ δ [ MASK ] R + ( 1 − ρ R ) ​ π R ] . \tilde{q}_{R}(r_{ij,t}\mid r_{ij,t-1})=(1-\beta_{t}^{R})\delta_{r_{ij,t-1}}+\beta_{t}^{R}\big[\rho_{R}\delta_{[\mathrm{MASK}]_{R}}+(1-\rho_{R})\pi_{R}\big]. (67) The edge-aware relation kernel remains q R ​ ( r i ​ j , t ∣ r i ​ j , t − 1 , e i ​ j , t ) = { q ~ R ​ ( r i ​ j , t ∣ r i ​ j , t − 1 ) , e i ​ j , t = 1 , δ 0 ​ ( r i ​ j , t ) , e i ​ j , t = 0 . q_{R}(r_{ij,t}\mid r_{ij,t-1},e_{ij,t})=\begin{cases}\tilde{q}_{R}(r_{ij,t}\mid r_{ij,t-1}),&e_{ij,t}=1,\\ \delta_{0}(r_{ij,t}),&e_{ij,t}=0.\end{cases} (68) Thus, we defined a structure-aware forward process over x t = ( V t , E t , R t + ) x_{t}=(V_{t},E_{t},R_{t}^{+}) such that q ⁡ ( x t ∣ x t − 1 ) = q V ​ q E ​ q R , q(x_{t}\mid x_{t-1})=q_{V}q_{E}q_{R}, with, q R ( R t ∣ R t − 1 , E t ) = ∏ i ​ j : e i ​ j , t = 1 q ~ R ( r i ​ j , t ∣ r i ​ j , t − 1 ) ∏ i ​ j : e i ​ j , t = 0 δ 0 ( r i ​ j , t ) . q_{R}(R_{t}\mid R_{t-1},E_{t})=\prod_{ij:e_{ij,t}=1}\tilde{q}_{R}(r_{ij,t}\mid r_{ij,t-1})\prod_{ij:e_{ij,t}=0}\delta_{0}(r_{ij,t}). (69) This construction: (i) preserves validity of the scene-graph state space, (ii) decouples structural sparsity from relation semantics, and (iii) prevents rare relations from competing with the no-edge class.

sections.heading: A.2 Factorized Reverse Sampler – Additional Details
sections.text: In this section, we discuss posterior derivation for the factorized scene graph model and refinements to the sampler at inference.

sections.heading: Discrete posterior for a categorical variable.
sections.text: [ 1 , 40 ] Consider a categorical variable z t ∈ { 1 , … , K } z_{t}\in\{1,\dots,K\} with forward transition matrices Q t , Q ¯ t = Q 1 Q 2 ⋯ Q t . \displaystyle Q_{t},\hskip 18.49988pt\bar{Q}_{t}=Q_{1}Q_{2}\cdots Q_{t}. (70) The one-step posterior conditioned on the clean variable z 0 z_{0} is q ⁡ ( z t − 1 = a ∣ z t = b , z 0 = c ) = q ⁡ ( z t = b ∣ z t − 1 = a ) ​ q ​ ( z t − 1 = a ∣ z 0 = c ) q ⁡ ( z t = b ∣ z 0 = c ) . \displaystyle q(z_{t-1}=a\mid z_{t}=b,z_{0}=c)=\frac{q(z_{t}=b\mid z_{t-1}=a)\,q(z_{t-1}=a\mid z_{0}=c)}{q(z_{t}=b\mid z_{0}=c)}. (71) Using the transition matrices, this becomes q ⁡ ( z t − 1 = a ∣ z t = b , z 0 = c ) = [ Q t ] a ​ b ​ [ Q ¯ t − 1 ] c ​ a [ Q ¯ t ] c ​ b . \displaystyle q(z_{t-1}=a\mid z_{t}=b,z_{0}=c)=\frac{[Q_{t}]_{ab}\,[\bar{Q}_{t-1}]_{ca}}{[\bar{Q}_{t}]_{cb}}. (72) Since z 0 z_{0} is unknown at sampling time, the model predicts a distribution p θ ​ ( z 0 = c ∣ x t ) . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(z_{0}=c\mid x_{t}). (73) The learned reverse posterior marginalizes over z 0 z_{0} : p θ ​ ( z t − 1 = a ∣ z t = b ) = ∑ c q ⁡ ( z t − 1 = a ∣ z t = b , z 0 = c ) ​ p θ ​ ( z 0 = c ∣ x t ) . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(z_{t-1}=a\mid z_{t}=b)=\sum_{c}q(z_{t-1}=a\mid z_{t}=b,z_{0}=c)\,p_{\theta}(z_{0}=c\mid x_{t}). (74) Equivalently, p θ ​ ( z t − 1 = a ∣ z t = b ) ∝ q ⁡ ( z t = b ∣ z t − 1 = a ) ​ ∑ c p θ ​ ( z 0 = c ∣ x t ) ​ q ​ ( z t − 1 = a ∣ z 0 = c ) . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(z_{t-1}=a\mid z_{t}=b)\propto q(z_{t}=b\mid z_{t-1}=a)\sum_{c}p_{\theta}(z_{0}=c\mid x_{t})q(z_{t-1}=a\mid z_{0}=c). (75)

sections.heading: Reverse factorization for scene graphs.
sections.text: For scene graphs, the clean state is x 0 = ( V 0 , E 0 , R 0 ) . \displaystyle x_{0}=(V_{0},E_{0},R_{0}). (76) Following the structured state space, we factorize the clean-state prediction as p θ ​ ( x 0 ∣ x t ) = p θ ​ ( V 0 , E 0 , R 0 ∣ x t ) . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(x_{0}\mid x_{t})=p_{\theta}(V_{0},E_{0},R_{0}\mid x_{t}). (77) A scene-graph-aware factorization is p θ ​ ( V 0 , E 0 , R 0 ∣ x t ) = p θ ​ ( V 0 ∣ x t ) ​ p θ ​ ( E 0 ∣ V 0 , x t ) ​ p θ ​ ( R 0 ∣ V 0 , E 0 , x t ) . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(V_{0},E_{0},R_{0}\mid x_{t})=p_{\theta}(V_{0}\mid x_{t})\,p_{\theta}(E_{0}\mid V_{0},x_{t})\,p_{\theta}(R_{0}\mid V_{0},E_{0},x_{t}). (78) This factorization follows the semantic structure of scene graphs: 1. object identities define the semantic entities in the graph, 2. directed edge existence determines which object pairs interact, 3. relation identities are meaningful only for active directed edges. Thus, relation prediction is conditioned on both object identity and edge existence.

sections.heading: Object reverse posterior.
sections.text: For each object variable v i v_{i} , the model predicts, p θ ​ ( v i , 0 = c ∣ x t ) . p_{\theta}(v_{i,0}=c\mid x_{t}). The reverse posterior is p θ ​ ( v i , t − 1 = a ∣ v i , t = b , x t ) = ∑ c q V ​ ( v i , t − 1 = a ∣ v i , t = b , v i , 0 = c ) ​ p θ ​ ( v i , 0 = c ∣ x t ) . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(v_{i,t-1}=a\mid v_{i,t}=b,x_{t})=\sum_{c}q_{V}(v_{i,t-1}=a\mid v_{i,t}=b,v_{i,0}=c)\,p_{\theta}(v_{i,0}=c\mid x_{t}). (79) Using the forward kernels, q V ​ ( v i , t − 1 = a ∣ v i , t = b , v i , 0 = c ) = [ Q t V ] a ​ b ​ [ Q ¯ t − 1 V ] c ​ a [ Q ¯ t V ] c ​ b . \displaystyle q_{V}(v_{i,t-1}=a\mid v_{i,t}=b,v_{i,0}=c)=\frac{[Q_{t}^{V}]_{ab}\,[\bar{Q}_{t-1}^{V}]_{ca}}{[\bar{Q}_{t}^{V}]_{cb}}. (80) Therefore, p θ ​ ( v i , t − 1 = a ∣ v i , t = b , x t ) = ∑ c [ Q t V ] a ​ b ​ [ Q ¯ t − 1 V ] c ​ a [ Q ¯ t V ] c ​ b ​ p θ ​ ( v i , 0 = c ∣ x t ) . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(v_{i,t-1}=a\mid v_{i,t}=b,x_{t})=\sum_{c}\frac{[Q_{t}^{V}]_{ab}\,[\bar{Q}_{t-1}^{V}]_{ca}}{[\bar{Q}_{t}^{V}]_{cb}}p_{\theta}(v_{i,0}=c\mid x_{t}). (81)

sections.heading: Edge reverse posterior.
sections.text: For each directed edge variable e i ​ j ∈ { 0 , 1 } e_{ij}\in\{0,1\} , the model predicts, p θ ​ ( e i ​ j , 0 = c ∣ V 0 , x t ) . p_{\theta}(e_{ij,0}=c\mid V_{0},x_{t}). The reverse posterior is p θ ​ ( e i ​ j , t − 1 = a ∣ e i ​ j , t = b , V 0 , x t ) = ∑ c q E ​ ( e i ​ j , t − 1 = a ∣ e i ​ j , t = b , e i ​ j , 0 = c ) ​ p θ ​ ( e i ​ j , 0 = c ∣ V 0 , x t ) , \displaystyle p_{\theta}(e_{ij,t-1}=a\mid e_{ij,t}=b,V_{0},x_{t})=\sum_{c}q_{E}(e_{ij,t-1}=a\mid e_{ij,t}=b,e_{ij,0}=c)p_{\theta}(e_{ij,0}=c\mid V_{0},x_{t}), (82) where q E ​ ( e i ​ j , t − 1 = a ∣ e i ​ j , t = b , e i ​ j , 0 = c ) = [ Q t E ] a ​ b ​ [ Q ¯ t − 1 E ] c ​ a [ Q ¯ t E ] c ​ b . \displaystyle q_{E}(e_{ij,t-1}=a\mid e_{ij,t}=b,e_{ij,0}=c)=\frac{[Q_{t}^{E}]_{ab}\,[\bar{Q}_{t-1}^{E}]_{ca}}{[\bar{Q}_{t}^{E}]_{cb}}. (83) Thus, p θ ​ ( e i ​ j , t − 1 = a ∣ e i ​ j , t = b , V 0 , x t ) = ∑ c [ Q t E ] a ​ b ​ [ Q ¯ t − 1 E ] c ​ a [ Q ¯ t E ] c ​ b ​ p θ ​ ( e i ​ j , 0 = c ∣ V 0 , x t ) . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(e_{ij,t-1}=a\mid e_{ij,t}=b,V_{0},x_{t})=\sum_{c}\frac{[Q_{t}^{E}]_{ab}\,[\bar{Q}_{t-1}^{E}]_{ca}}{[\bar{Q}_{t}^{E}]_{cb}}p_{\theta}(e_{ij,0}=c\mid V_{0},x_{t}). (84)

sections.heading: Edge-gated relation reverse posterior.
sections.text: Relations are only meaningful on active directed edges. Since the forward relation corruption is conditioned on the current edge state e i ​ j , t e_{ij,t} , the reverse relation posterior must distinguish three cases depending on ( e i ​ j , t − 1 , e i ​ j , t ) (e_{ij,t-1},e_{ij,t}) . Let the denoiser output clean relation logits after edge and object predictions, ϵ θ R ​ ( x t , t , V t − 1 , E t − 1 ) i ​ j ∈ ℝ K rel , \displaystyle\epsilon_{\theta}^{R}(x_{t},t,V_{t-1},E_{t-1})_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{K_{\mathrm{rel}}}, (85) and the predicted clean relation distribution on active edges is, p θ ​ ( r i ​ j , 0 = c ∣ x t , V t − 1 , E t − 1 ) = softmax ​ ( ϵ θ R ​ ( x t , t , V t − 1 , E t − 1 ) i ​ j ) c . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(r_{ij,0}=c\mid x_{t},V_{t-1},E_{t-1})=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\epsilon_{\theta}^{R}(x_{t},t,V_{t-1},E_{t-1})_{ij}\right)_{c}. (86) Case 1: Edge absent at t − 1 t-1 . If e i ​ j , t − 1 = 0 , e_{ij,t-1}=0, then the relation is deterministically null: p θ ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 = 0 ∣ e i ​ j , t − 1 = 0 , x t ) = 1 . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(r_{ij,t-1}=0\mid e_{ij,t-1}=0,x_{t})=1. (87) Case 2: Edge active at both t − 1 t-1 and t t . If e i ​ j , t − 1 = 1 , e i ​ j , t = 1 , e_{ij,t-1}=1,\hskip 9.24994pte_{ij,t}=1, then relation corruption was active in the forward process. Therefore we can use the standard discrete posterior over positive relation labels: p θ ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 = a ∣ r i ​ j , t = b , e i ​ j , t − 1 = 1 , e i ​ j , t = 1 , x t ) \displaystyle p_{\theta}(r_{ij,t-1}=a\mid r_{ij,t}=b,e_{ij,t-1}=1,e_{ij,t}=1,x_{t}) = ∑ c q R ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 = a ∣ r i ​ j , t = b , r i ​ j , 0 = c ) \displaystyle=\sum_{c}q_{R}(r_{ij,t-1}=a\mid r_{ij,t}=b,r_{ij,0}=c) (88) p θ ​ ( r i ​ j , 0 = c ∣ x t , V t − 1 , E t − 1 ) , \displaystyle p_{\theta}(r_{ij,0}=c\mid x_{t},V_{t-1},E_{t-1}), where q R ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 = a ∣ r i ​ j , t = b , r i ​ j , 0 = c ) = [ Q t R ] a ​ b ​ [ Q ¯ t − 1 R ] c ​ a [ Q ¯ t R ] c ​ b . \displaystyle q_{R}(r_{ij,t-1}=a\mid r_{ij,t}=b,r_{ij,0}=c)=\frac{[Q_{t}^{R}]_{ab}\,[\bar{Q}_{t-1}^{R}]_{ca}}{[\bar{Q}_{t}^{R}]_{cb}}. (89) Equivalently, p θ ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 = a ∣ r i ​ j , t = b , e i ​ j , t − 1 = 1 , e i ​ j , t = 1 , x t ) \displaystyle p_{\theta}(r_{ij,t-1}=a\mid r_{ij,t}=b,e_{ij,t-1}=1,e_{ij,t}=1,x_{t}) ∝ q R ​ ( r i ​ j , t = b ∣ r i ​ j , t − 1 = a ) \displaystyle\propto q_{R}(r_{ij,t}=b\mid r_{ij,t-1}=a) (90) ∑ c p θ ​ ( r i ​ j , 0 = c ∣ x t , V t − 1 , E t − 1 ) ​ q R ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 = a ∣ r i ​ j , 0 = c ) . \displaystyle\sum_{c}p_{\theta}(r_{ij,0}=c\mid x_{t},V_{t-1},E_{t-1})q_{R}(r_{ij,t-1}=a\mid r_{ij,0}=c). Case 3: Edge reactivates in the reverse step. The key sampler modification for the factorized setting is in addressing this case. If e i ​ j , t − 1 = 1 , e i ​ j , t = 0 , e_{ij,t-1}=1,\hskip 9.24994pte_{ij,t}=0, then the current relation r i ​ j , t = 0 r_{ij,t}=0 is caused deterministically by the absence of the current edge. Hence r i ​ j , t r_{ij,t} carries no semantic information about the positive relation at t − 1 t-1 . We therefore use the predictive marginal obtained by propagating the denoiser’s clean relation prediction to timestep t − 1 t-1 : p θ ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 = a ∣ e i ​ j , t − 1 = 1 , e i ​ j , t = 0 , x t ) = ∑ c q R ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 = a ∣ r i ​ j , 0 = c ) ​ p θ ​ ( r i ​ j , 0 = c ∣ x t , V t − 1 , E t − 1 ) . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(r_{ij,t-1}=a\mid e_{ij,t-1}=1,e_{ij,t}=0,x_{t})=\sum_{c}q_{R}(r_{ij,t-1}=a\mid r_{ij,0}=c)p_{\theta}(r_{ij,0}=c\mid x_{t},V_{t-1},E_{t-1}). (91) Using the relation marginal transition matrix, q R ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 = a ∣ r i ​ j , 0 = c ) = [ Q ¯ t − 1 R ] c ​ a , \displaystyle q_{R}(r_{ij,t-1}=a\mid r_{ij,0}=c)=[\bar{Q}_{t-1}^{R}]_{ca}, (92) so p θ ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 = a ∣ e i ​ j , t − 1 = 1 , e i ​ j , t = 0 , x t ) = ∑ c [ Q ¯ t − 1 R ] c ​ a ​ p θ ​ ( r i ​ j , 0 = c ∣ x t , V t − 1 , E t − 1 ) . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(r_{ij,t-1}=a\mid e_{ij,t-1}=1,e_{ij,t}=0,x_{t})=\sum_{c}[\bar{Q}_{t-1}^{R}]_{ca}p_{\theta}(r_{ij,0}=c\mid x_{t},V_{t-1},E_{t-1}). (93) Thus the full edge-gated relation sampler is p θ ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 ∣ r i ​ j , t , e i ​ j , t − 1 , e i ​ j , t , x t ) = { δ 0 ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 ) , e i ​ j , t − 1 = 0 , p θ post ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 ∣ r i ​ j , t , x t ) , e i ​ j , t − 1 = 1 , e i ​ j , t = 1 , p θ marg ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 ∣ x t ) , e i ​ j , t − 1 = 1 , e i ​ j , t = 0 . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(r_{ij,t-1}\mid r_{ij,t},e_{ij,t-1},e_{ij,t},x_{t})=\begin{cases}\delta_{0}(r_{ij,t-1}),&e_{ij,t-1}=0,\\[6.0pt] p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{post}}(r_{ij,t-1}\mid r_{ij,t},x_{t}),&e_{ij,t-1}=1,\ e_{ij,t}=1,\\[6.0pt] p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{marg}}(r_{ij,t-1}\mid x_{t}),&e_{ij,t-1}=1,\ e_{ij,t}=0.\end{cases} (94)

sections.heading: Structured reverse transition.
sections.text: Combining the object, edge, and relation posterior updates gives the structured reverse transition, p θ ​ ( x t − 1 ∣ x t ) = p θ ​ ( V t − 1 ∣ x t ) ​ p θ ​ ( E t − 1 ∣ V t − 1 , x t ) ​ p θ ​ ( R t − 1 ∣ V t − 1 , E t − 1 , x t ) . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(x_{t-1}\mid x_{t})=p_{\theta}(V_{t-1}\mid x_{t})\,p_{\theta}(E_{t-1}\mid V_{t-1},x_{t})\,p_{\theta}(R_{t-1}\mid V_{t-1},E_{t-1},x_{t}). (95) p θ ​ ( x t − 1 ∣ x t ) = ∏ i p θ ​ ( v i , t − 1 ∣ v i , t , x t ) ​ ∏ i ≠ j p θ ​ ( e i ​ j , t − 1 ∣ e i ​ j , t , V t − 1 , x t ) ​ ∏ i ≠ j p θ ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 ∣ r i ​ j , t , e i ​ j , t − 1 , V t − 1 , E t − 1 , x t ) . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(x_{t-1}\mid x_{t})=\prod_{i}p_{\theta}(v_{i,t-1}\mid v_{i,t},x_{t})\prod_{i\neq j}p_{\theta}(e_{ij,t-1}\mid e_{ij,t},V_{t-1},x_{t})\prod_{i\neq j}p_{\theta}(r_{ij,t-1}\mid r_{ij,t},e_{ij,t-1},V_{t-1},E_{t-1},x_{t}). (96) The final relation factor in Eqn. 96 is edge-gated (Eqn. 94 ). Proposition. Validity preservation of the reverse sampler: If the reverse sampler uses the edge-gated relation posterior above, then every sampled state x t − 1 x_{t-1} satisfies e i ​ j , t − 1 = 0 ⇒ r i ​ j , t − 1 = 0 . \displaystyle e_{ij,t-1}=0\Rightarrow r_{ij,t-1}=0. (97) For any directed pair ( i , j ) (i,j) , suppose e i ​ j , t − 1 = 0 . e_{ij,t-1}=0. By definition of the edge-gated relation posterior, p θ ​ ( r i ​ j , t − 1 = 0 ∣ e i ​ j , t − 1 = 0 , x t ) = 1 . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(r_{ij,t-1}=0\mid e_{ij,t-1}=0,x_{t})=1. (98) Therefore the only relation value with nonzero probability is r i ​ j , t − 1 = 0 r_{ij,t-1}=0 . Hence e i ​ j , t − 1 = 0 ⇒ r i ​ j , t − 1 = 0 . \displaystyle e_{ij,t-1}=0\Rightarrow r_{ij,t-1}=0. (99) Thus the sampled state remains in the constrained scene graph space.

sections.heading: Sampling Process.
sections.text: At each reverse timestep t t , we perform: 1. Predict object clean-state probabilities: p θ ​ ( V 0 ∣ x t ) . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(V_{0}\mid x_{t}). (100) Sample or decode V t − 1 ∼ p θ ​ ( V t − 1 ∣ x t ) \displaystyle V_{t-1}\sim p_{\theta}(V_{t-1}\mid x_{t}) (101) using the object posterior. 2. Predict edge clean-state probabilities conditioned on recovered objects: p θ ​ ( E 0 ∣ V t − 1 , x t ) . \displaystyle p_{\theta}(E_{0}\mid V_{t-1},x_{t}). sections.text: ■ \blacksquare Graph Metrics. A scene graph is defined as G = ( V , E , R ) G=(V,E,R) , where V = { v i } i = 1 N V V=\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{V}} are node labels with v i ∈ 𝒱 v_{i}\in\mathcal{V} , E = { e i ​ j } i , j = 1 N E E=\{e_{ij}\}_{i,j=1}^{N_{E}} is binary edge existence with e i ​ j ∈ { 0 , 1 } e_{ij}\in\{0,1\} , and R = { r i ​ j } i , j = 1 N R R=\{r_{ij}\}_{i,j=1}^{N_{R}} are relation labels with r i ​ j ∈ ℛ r_{ij}\in\mathcal{R} and r i ​ j = 0 r_{ij}=0 indicating no relation. Let p data p_{\text{data}} denote the empirical distribution of real graphs and p θ p_{\theta} denote the distribution of generated graphs.

sections.text: We highlight DiScGraph ’s capability to learn grounding signals from scene graphs in Figure 18 . The text-conditioned scene graphs are converted to layouts by the layout head, and these layouts are used to generated images using GLIGEN [ 19 ] model. sections.heading: A.8 Broader Impacts
sections.text: DiScGraph improves text-to-image generation by learning a structured scene graph prior using a factorized discrete diffusion model. At the same time, it introduces certain risks. It could be misused to create deceptive or misleading visuals, contributing to the spread of misinformation. When applied to depictions of public figures, it may compromise personal privacy. Moreover, the generated content can raise concerns around copyright and intellectual property.

Recent work suggests that conditioning image generation on scene graphs improves compositional fidelity compared to text-only prompting. However, since users typically provide text rather than structured graphs, a key challenge is to generate scene graphs from natural language. Prior work on discrete diffusion has demonstrated success in generating generic graphs such as molecules and circuits, but fails to account for the hierarchical structure and strong dependencies between objects, edges, and relations in scene graphs. We address this limitation by introducing a dependency-aware, hierarchically constrained discrete diffusion model for scene graph generation. Our approach decouples structure and semantics across the forward and reverse processes, enabling the model to capture conditional dependencies. At inference time, we perform training-free conditioning to sample text-aligned scene graphs. We evaluate our method on standard SG benchmarks and demonstrate improvements over both continuous and discrete graph generation baselines across graph and layout metrics. When fed to downstream image generation, our approach yields improved compositional alignment compared to text-to-image models, particularly in multi-object scenarios. 1 Introduction Text-to-image (T2I) models have made remarkable progress in generating images from user-specified prompts, but user expectations are rising just as quickly. As prompts become longer and more complex, multiple lines of attack are being explored to improve compositional fidelity and alignment. Figure 1: Image I I and its scene graph G G . Objects are pink nodes and relations are labels on edges. One promising direction is to generate images from scene graphs (SGs)—see Fig. 1 —where visual objects are represented as nodes and their relationships as edges. Recent papers Xu et al. (2024) ; Farshad et al. (2023) ; Thanh-Nhan et al. (2025) ; Shen and Lin (2025) suggest that SG-conditioned image generation p ⁡ ( I | G ) p(I|G) can be more effective, particularly in compositional settings. While these gains are largely empirical, they are intuitively justified: text-based conditioning lacks explicit relational constraints, often leading to compositional inconsistencies. In contrast, scene graphs provide an explicit factorization over objects and relations, offering a structured prior that is difficult to encode in text embeddings. Given this momentum, a natural question arises: how can scene graphs (SG) be generated from text prompts? While text-to-SG mapping may appear deterministic, it is inherently multi-modal due to the ambiguity and under-specification of natural language. For example, a prompt such as “a person and a surfboard” does not specify their relationship; the person could be on, beside, or holding the surfboard. Multiple valid SGs may correspond to the same prompt, necessitating modeling a conditional distribution p ⁡ ( G | T ) p(G|T) rather than predicting a single deterministic output. Motivated by this, we propose to learn the manifold of scene graphs using discrete diffusion models, and then perform conditional generation of SGs from text prompts. However, this presents a fundamental challenge: scene graphs are significantly more complex than generic graphs. They exhibit long-tailed vocabularies, strong conditional dependencies between objects and relations, and global structural constraints. Injecting these properties into discrete diffusion remains underexplored. A key limitation of existing discrete diffusion approaches Vignac et al. (2023) —designed for generic graphs like molecules or traffic networks—is that they rely on parameterizations that treat nodes and edges as independent categorical variables in both the forward and reverse processes. With scene graphs, such independence assumptions break due to the inherent conditional dependencies, such as the hierarchical structure where objects determine edges and edges determine relations. Our key insight is that scene graphs require a hierarchically constrained discrete diffusion process , where structure and semantics are modeled with explicit conditional dependencies rather than independent categorical transitions.
